questions.question: Which of the following components is explicitly mentioned in the context as part of a general‑purpose processor’s basic architecture?
questions.explanation:
The context specifies an Instruction Register (IR) of 16‑bit width as a design element of the GPP [Page 106].

---

questions.question: According to the design example, what is the width of the Program Counter (PC) in the described general‑purpose processor?
questions.explanation:
The example lists a 16‑bit Program Counter (PC) as part of the processor design [Page 106].

---

questions.question: Which instruction format from the context uses the first byte “0000 Rn” to move data from memory to a register?
questions.explanation:
The table shows “MOV Rn, direct” with first byte “0000 Rn” performing Rn = M[direct] [Page 107].

---

questions.question: In the instruction set described, which operation writes the contents of a register to a direct memory address?
questions.explanation:
“MOV direct, Rn” has first byte “0001 Rn” and stores Rn into M[direct] [Page 107].

questions.question: How many distinct instruction categories (data‑transfer, arithmetic, jump) are stated as being supported by the example general‑purpose processor design?
questions.explanation:
The design example calls for four data‑transfer, two arithmetic, and one jump instruction, totaling three categories [Page 106].

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a general‑purpose processor (GPP) as defined in the context?

options.A: A CPU integrated with fixed memory and I/O on a single chip
options.B: A flexible, programmable core used for multiple applications
options.C: A processor optimized for signal‑processing tasks only
options.D: A specialized ASIC for a single function

questions.explanation:
The context lists GPPs as “Flexible, programmable cores used for multiple applications” [Page 40].

---

questions.question: What is the instruction size specified for the example GPP design?
questions.explanation:
The example explicitly states a 16‑bit instruction size [Page 106].

---

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the relationship between a GPP and a single‑purpose processor is correct according to the text?

options.A: A GPP cannot be designed using the same steps as a single‑purpose processor.
options.B: A GPP is essentially a programmable single‑purpose processor that executes stored instructions.
options.C: A GPP always has a fixed instruction set, unlike single‑purpose processors.
options.D: A GPP does not use program memory for instruction storage.

questions.explanation:
The text notes that a GPP “is essentially a programmable single‑purpose processor—it executes a sequence of instructions stored in program memory” [Page 105].

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a data‑transfer instruction with its described operation?
questions.explanation:
The table lists “MOV @Rn, Rm” with operation M[Rn] = Rm [Page 107].

questions.question: According to the context, which category distinguishes a microprocessor (MPU) from a microcontroller (MCU)?

options.A: MPUs include integrated I/O peripherals, while MCUs do not.
options.B: MPUs consist only of a CPU and require external memory, whereas MCUs combine CPU, memory, and I/O on one chip.
options.C: MCUs are always 64‑bit, while MPUs are 32‑bit.
options.D: MPUs are designed for embedded systems, MCUs are for desktop computers.

questions.explanation: The comparison table shows that an MPU is “CPU only; needs external memory” whereas an MCU is “CPU + memory + I/O on one chip” [Page 43].
